item.title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
item.description:
Worth a look new result — In-place integer modular multiplication modulo a power of two, standard integer multiplication, and modular inversion modulo a power of two run in O(n1+ϵ) gates for any ϵ>0 with zero ancilla qubits (or ⌈log2⁡m⌉ ancillas for standard multiplication by a general quantum multiplier).

Grade 0.440 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden

Figure

The plot displays the number of modular multiplications required to perform in-place inversion modulo 2m as the number of clean ancilla qubits s increases.

Asks

Can in-place and ancilla-free quantum arithmetic algorithms achieve subquadratic gate complexity?

Before

Existing in-place, ancilla-free integer multiplication and modular multiplication algorithms required Ω(n2) gates.

But

Multipliers restricted to odd integers for modular operations and non-zero integers for standard multiplication; registers sized with m=O(n); small ϵ introduces large constant factors.

Tools

phase-encoded fast integer multiplication · controlled and parametrized quantum Fourier transform · abstract quantum circuit model

Abstract

Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using O(n^(1+ε)) gates and no ancilla qubits, for any ε>0. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using O(n^(1+ε)) gates for any ε>0, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using O(n^(1+ε)) gates and no ancilla qubits, for any ε>0. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

item.title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Classical complexity of quantum state transmission equals classical communication cost for correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments. For d-dimensional states under isotropic noise, classical complexity scales exponentially with d and as power-law (1−v)−(d−1) with inverse noise; at d=16 and visibility v=90%, simulation requires ≥1015 symbols.

Grade 0.440 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Elna Svegborn, Alexander Bernal, Armin Tavakoli

Figure

Schematic of the prepare-and-broadcast and related communication scenarios establishing equivalence between classical message complexity and quantum correlation simulation.

Asks

How much classical communication is required to transmit a given set of quantum states using shared randomness?

But

Isotropic white noise model; finite sets certified via scalable linear programming outer/inner approximations strictly for qubits.

Tools

classical communication models · semidefinite programming · convex subgradient methods · Bloch sphere polytope approximations

Abstract

Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

item.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
item.description:
Worth a look new method — End-to-end quantum solver for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation achieves total quantum gate cost polylogarithmic in grid points Ng and quasilinear in 1/ε, matching classical preprocessing cost in polylog⁡(Ng,1/ε).

Grade 0.439 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin K. Brennen, Barry C. Sanders, Alán Aspuru-Guzik

Figure

Normalized computational cost scaling versus spatial grid points Ng and target accuracy 1/ε, contrasting polylogarithmic quantum gate cost against classical geometric multigrid scaling.

Asks

Can an end-to-end quantum algorithm solve a practical variable-coefficient partial differential equation with rigorous gate costs, classical inputs, and classical outputs without relying on abstract oracles?

But

Treats algorithmic estimation error ε independently of spatial discretization error; applies to linearized regime with bounded variable coefficients.

Tools

diagonal wavelet preconditioning · block encoding via multiscale refinement · quantum linear system algorithms · fixed-point amplitude amplification · quantum phase estimation

Abstract

Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points N_g and the inverse of the desired accuracy ε, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in N_g and quasilinear in 1/ε. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in N_g and 1/ε. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with N_g over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.
